title: Making the Case
sub: Grades 5–8 · ELA · Poster 1 as an argument
objective: Students will read poster 1, *Black History Month*, as an argument. They will find its central claim (*“Despite significant progress in race relations, Black History Month remains a vital tool for transformation.”*) and the concession that opens it, tell its reasons from its evidence and examples, and explain how words such as *historical amnesia* and *resilience* give it weight. Then they will weigh its evidence and write an argument of their own.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Poster 1 does not only tell the story of Black History Month; it argues that the month still matters. Learning to find a claim, test its evidence and make a case of your own is how a reader becomes a citizen who can weigh what they are told.

materials: Poster 1: page 3 of this plan, or the poster online, with its readings
questions: Who is the poster talking to? How can you tell?
What does the writer want readers to think, and to do?
Which sentence would you underline if you only had one? Why?
What question would you ask the writer about the surveys?
questionsLabel: Questions to ask about the poster
connection: **Online,** the poster walks through its text panel by panel, with each part read aloud and a *Talk about it* question for each part. **In the exhibition,** read poster 1 beside poster 2: both make a case.

steps.title: Which sentence argues?
script: Play the three sentences that open the poster’s three parts, without showing the text. Ask: *“Three sentences open the poster’s three parts. Which one is arguing?”* The first tells a story (Woodson created Negro History Week in 1926). The second and third make claims someone could disagree with. *“Today we read this poster the way a debater would.”*

screen.question: Three sentences open the poster’s three parts. Which one is arguing?

steps.purpose: Hear the poster before reading it, and tell telling from arguing.
students: Which one tells? Which ones argue?

steps.title: The claim
script: Show the claim: *“Despite significant progress in race relations, Black History Month remains a vital tool for transformation.”* Ask: *“Why might a writer begin a claim with “Despite”?”* The writer admits a point first (*significant progress*), then argues that the month is still needed. That move is a **concession**: it answers a reader who disagrees before they speak.

screen.text: Despite significant progress in race relations, Black History Month remains a vital tool for transformation.

steps.purpose: Find the claim, and see how the concession prepares for it.
students: Why might a writer begin a claim with “Despite”?
What would someone who disagreed say?

steps.title: How the case is built
script: Read the rest of the poster on page 3 and give each sentence a job. Two reasons follow the claim: the month is *a reminder* that counters *historical amnesia*, and it can *bridge these gaps*. One sentence offers evidence: *“Surveys reveal a concerning lack of awareness about slavery’s impact, even among African Americans.”* Ask: *whose surveys?* The poster does not say. A second claim (preservation) is backed by examples: historical sites and artifacts given to museums.

cells: Despite significant progress in race relations, Black History Month remains a vital tool for transformation.

It serves as a reminder of the struggles and achievements of African Americans, countering historical amnesia and ensuring that crucial aspects of history, like slavery and the fight for civil rights, are not forgotten.
Surveys reveal a concerning lack of awareness about slavery’s impact, even among African Americans.

By fostering discussion and reflection, Black History Month can bridge these gaps, inspire a deeper connection to the past, and promote an understanding of the resilience and contributions of Black individuals throughout history.
Beyond education, Black History Month reinforces the importance of preserving African American culture and heritage.
From safeguarding historical sites to encouraging donations of artifacts to museums, cultural preservation ensures that Black history is recognized and valued.
Additionally, the celebration provides inspiration by honoring figures like Martin Luther King Jr., Harriet Tubman, and Langston Hughes.
As society evolves, Black History Month continues to be relevant, reminding all Americans that understanding the past is essential for shaping a more just and inclusive future.

steps.purpose: Tell each sentence’s job: reason, evidence, example or conclusion.

steps.title: Words with weight
script: Put up five words: *historical amnesia, racial uplift, resilience, preservation, transformation.* Ask what each means, and why a writer would choose *amnesia*, a word for an illness of memory, over *forgetting*.

screen.text:
Historical amnesia
Racial uplift
Resilience
Preservation
Transformation

steps.purpose: Notice how chosen words make an argument stronger.
students: Why might the writer have chosen it?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three read the poster’s argument, then make one of their own.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Give five of the poster’s sentences their jobs, match five strong words to their meanings, and write a three-sentence argument from a frame.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Map the poster’s argument in a table, explain its concession, say what they would need to know to trust its survey sentence, and write a paragraph arguing why the month matters at their school.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Rank the poster’s reasons, weigh the effect of its word choices, test its unsupported evidence, and write a two-paragraph argument that answers a reader who disagrees.

steps.purpose: Read and make arguments at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three read the poster’s argument, then make one of their own.

steps.title: Read it back
script: Three students, one from each level, read their claim and best reason aloud. Ask: *“Which reason in the poster is strongest? Which would you add?”*

screen.question: Which reason in the poster is strongest? Which would you add?

steps.purpose: Share arguments, and weigh the poster’s reasons against the class’s own.
students: Name the reason you think is strongest.

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the objectives back on the screen, asked as questions: *“Can you now…?”* For each one, students show a thumb up, sideways or down. Ask one student to answer each aloud; for the last, ask a Red Level reader.
